Commentary.Commentary: Welcome for India's response with the bat. The Proteas form a huddle where Kyle Verreynne is seen offering words of motivation to his teammates. KL Rahul and Yashasvi Jaiswal are the two openers for India. Marco Jansen has the new ball and is raring to go. India need 549 runs to win, which realistically looks unrealistic to achieve. South Africa are just 10 good balls away from executing a whitewash. Jaiswal to face. Here we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

The Indians looked flat and deflated with the ball. They didn't get wickets in clusters on a surface that is still decent enough to bat. But coming into this penultimate day, where spinners bowled for the maximum part, the wear and tear began to get more and more evident with the ball spitting and turning off the track wildly. Yet the South African batters produced a batting masterclass worthy of high praise. They just didn't give India any chance and produced a masterclass in batting. Jadeja finally broke through to dismiss de Zorzi after a prolonged struggle, but the door to a potential collapse was slammed shut immediately. From that point onward, it became simply a matter of waiting for the inevitable declaration. Jadeja was the most successful bowler for India with a 4-fer, while Sundar too, got a good bit of purchase, but that was it.

Dominance would be an understatement to describe South Africa's performance in this Test match, and in the series overall. They have completely snuffed India out of the contest and only two possibilities remain. A South African win, which earns them 12 crucial points in this WTC cycle. Or a draw, where 4 points will be shared between both teams. Except for Temba Bavuma, each South African batter got the start and went past double figures. They got into their 30s and 40s, but Tristan Stubbs was the only one who got beyond that half-century mark.

And there comes the signal from Temba Bavuma in the Proteas dressing room. SOUTH AFRICA HAVE DECLARED ON 260/5. The wait was for Tristan Stubbs to get to his third Test century, which he missed by a hit. Also, this is the biggest lead South Africa have ever got against India, in Test cricket, in the third innings. KL Rahul and Yashasvi Jaiswal rush into the dressing room to pad up as they have very little time for the turnaround.

Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for the third and final session of the day. And the assumptions of South Africa declaring have been put to bed, as the tourists have decided to continue piling misery on the hosts. 'Chin up' is what the message would be for the Indian players, who form a huddle before scattering out to take the field. 29 overs remaining in the day, and if South Africa finally decide to pull the plug on their innings in between, there will be a ten-minute break between the change of innings, which means, a couple of overs or so will be lost if that happens. Well then, Tristan Stubbs and Wiaan Mulder walk out to the crease to resume batting. Ravindra Jadeja will get us underway in the last session. Mulder to face. Here we go...
... DAY 4, SESSION 3 ...

Not that the Indian bowlers didn't create opportunities. They did on the tiring surface. But you have to give it to the South African batters for applying themselves extremely well. Will the declaration come during this Lunch interval from the visitors? Or will South Africa decide to bat on? We will get to know as the final session of Day 4 begins at 2.03 pm IST (8.33 am GMT). Stay tuned.

Tony de Zorzi injected momentum with his adventurous sweeps and reverse sweeps, while Stubbs adopted a more patient approach and built his innings steadily. The pitch grew increasingly unpredictable as the day wore on. More deliveries spat and turned sharply, with several fizzing past the outside edge by the narrowest of margins. Still, they bridged a 101-run partnership before Tony de Zorzi was finally dismissed by Jadeja. But Stubbs kept mounting on the runs. and multiplied the frustrations in that Indian camp with his gritty half century. Wiaan Mulder joined in alliance with him and the two looked unfazed for their 42-run stand and went unbeaten into the break.

After losing three wickets in backend of the morning session, Tristan Stubbs and Tony de Zorzi found their rhythm against the Indian spinners. They emerged for the afternoon with renewed determination and a sharper game plan against the turning ball. Their footwork became alert in defense while they kept the scoreboard ticking along nicely. The Indian spinners toiled relentlessly in tandem but couldn't break through as the batters seized control.

Another session has flown by in this second Test, and another one bossed up by South Africa. Out of 10 sessions, they have dominated nine of those. 30 overs bowled, the Proteas managed to add 113 runs, and lost just a solitary wicket this afternoon and just kept piling the misery on the Indians. Very tired legs in that Indian camp and understandably so. They have been on the field for all four days, and for more than 220 overs, but have got very few rewards. Whether South Africa declare or decide to continue after the Lunch break, we will come to know in a short while. They have already got their lead past that 500-run figure and the question is, how many more do they need to bowl India out?

Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back. It's time for the second session to unfold. Tristan Stubbs and Tony de Zorzi have added 30 runs in just 51 balls. South Africa lead by 395 runs. This session is key for both teams. The players are out in the middle. Kuldeep Yadav to bowl first after the break.
...DAY 4, SESSION 2...

South Africa won't mind much as they have added 81 runs to the bigger picture and sit in a pretty comfortable position. Tristan Stubbs has been through the thick of the action, busy in the middle, taking some risky singles but have made sure the scoreboards keep ticking. The question is how much South Africa will be willing to accept. Maybe 450, maybe 500, maybe one more session. Who knows! Time will tell the answer. Join us for the Post-Tea session at 11.20 am IST (5.50 am GMT). Cheers!

Mohammed Siraj was given just one over in his opening spell before Washington Sundar replaced him. Sundar and Ravindra Jadeja bowled in tandem with a lot more control in their line and lengths, mainly attacking the stumps. Ravindra Jadeja removed Ryan Rickelton and, with a magic delivery, got the big fish in Aiden Markram as well. Washington Sundar was rewarded for his fine bowling as well, picking Temba Bavuma with a rank turner.

After 9 sessions, India have finally arrived on the Assamese shores as they have dominated a session in this match. Oh hang on, meanwhile South Africa have stretched their lead to 395 runs, which is a daunting task knowing the hosts are trailing in the series. However, talking about the morning of Day 4, India deserve some praise. A lot was talked about the speed comparison between the spinners from both teams. India, bowling at higher speeds got a lesser degree of turn. Today, they stuck to their speed but bowled with more energy and with conviction to claim prized wickets.
Floated fuller and on middle, Tristan Stubbs takes a massive stride forward and smothers the spin. And that will be TEA on Day 4!

Commentary.Commentary: DRINKS BREAK. 40/1 for South Africa in the opening hour of the fourth day. After brief spells of pace from Bumrah and Siraj, spin was brought in tandem. Both the turners, Jadeja and Sundar haven't given much away. They have bowled with control and the main template has been the way they have constantly targeted the stumps, denying easy runs. But overall, the Saffas will be happy with where they stand in this game. The pitch is still looking really good for batting, with minimal wear and tear. For India, it is all about keep chipping away at the wickets regularly and to turn the session blue, they will need at least a couple of wickets, or even more, in the next hour before the Tea break.

Commentary.Commentary: In all readiness for Day 4 to commence. The umpires and players punctually make their way out to the middle. The Indian players form a huddle before they spread out to take their respective fielding positions. Ryan Rickelton and Aiden Markram are the openers as well as the overnight batters for South Africa. And Jasprit Bumrah (3-0-13-0) is all set to get us underway with the first over. A massively crucial half an hour on the cards. The question is, with the Saffas add quick runs straightaway or will they take their own time? But for India, they are not only running against time, but also need to get regular breakthroughs to restrict the tourists to as little as they can. Rickelton to face, with three slips and a gully in place. Here we go...

PITCH REPORT - Deep Dasgupta and Shaun Pollock are having a look at the Day 4 surface in Guwahati. Deep starts by pointing out that it is a pleasant morning. Shaun Pollock observes a few little foot holes, but nothing extravagant. He then shares about the average pace and turn that spinners from both sides generated. Detailing further into it, he highlights that the Indian spinners were a bit quicker through the air, with an average pace of about 90 kph, and got less turn. Whereas the South African spinners extracted more turn and grip by offering much air to the ball, with an average pace of 83.5 kph, and were clever with their variations as well. He walks to the centre of the pitch and reckons that this is the most even bounce he has seen in India for a while. Adds that Marco Jansen used his height and bounce to great effect. Stresses that he will need to do more of that, but also feels that India will deal with it better in the second innings.

A few minutes back, in the team huddle, the Indian head coach, Gautam Gambhir, engaged in a lengthy and animated conversation. He pumped up the motivation in his players. And now, he walks up to the pitch to have a closer look. What does it look like? Pitch report coming up...

It’s been a long Test for the Indian bowlers. They have bowled on each of the three days so far in the match, and will have to bowl on this fourth day as well. So, the workload has been immense. They've got a massive job ahead and will be desperate to make early inroads in the morning session. The Proteas, meanwhile, will resume effectively on 314 without loss. That scoreline alone tells you how deep a hole India have dug themselves into. The big question now is how long South Africa will bat before pulling the trigger on a declaration and putting India back in to face the music. Or do the Indians have it in them to bundle this Proteas batting unit? Another absorbing day of cricket is about to begin. So stay tuned as the morning session of the day will give us a clear picture of where this is heading. The first ball is just a few minutes away.

Now onto the execution side of things. The Proteas bowlers have nailed the pace and variations this pitch demands. Marco Jansen peppered the batters with hostile short stuff that constantly had them hopping, while Simon Harmer and Keshav Maharaj gave the ball plenty of air to dip, grip and bounce off the surface to get the rewards. Most crucially, all of them hammering away at the stumps, forcing the Indian batters to make decisions and play shots they didn't always want to. India's bowlers, to be fair, haven't been as consistent with that approach. And crucially, it all underpinned in those 68 balls that caused the procession. Sure, the choice of shots will be put under scrutiny as well.

The pitch isn't a minefield by any means, and Kuldeep and Sundar’s late resistance on Monday, in an alliance of 208 balls, proved exactly that. Sure, it's on the slower side, and after being used for three days, it is naturally bound to show some wear and tear. But overall, there's still something in it for both bat and ball. Yet somehow it felt like South Africa and India have been playing on completely different surfaces. Where the Proteas batted rather comfortably for over 150 overs, India crumbled in almost half that time. So one can opine that the application has been the key difference maker that separates the two sides.

And… we are back again. This second Test has moved at its own pace in Guwahati, with South Africa holding all the aces and are smelling blood. Nine sessions down, the tourists have bossed up eight of those. Just shows how dominant they have been, not only in this game, but throughout the series. India, on the other hand, have looked dull and are on the mat yet again. By any stretch of imagination, a win looks almost impossible for them, with a draw as the best possible result. They surely will have to dig deep when they come out to bat again. On that note, we welcome you all to our coverage of the fourth day of this second and final Test.

Right then, another day that belonged to South Africa. Disappointment for the Indians as they are staring at another potential whitewash at home. Still early to say, but the writing seems to be on the wall. The best result they can squeeze out from this one is to drag it into a draw. But for that, if and when the Proteas declare, or the Indians bowl the tourists out, they will still have to come out to bat and dig deep. South Africa will effectively begin Day 4 with 314 on the board, and they will aim to stretch the game far away from India's reach. Action will resume on 25th November, Tuesday, with the first ball scheduled to be bowled at 9 am IST (3.30 am GMT). But do join us for the buildup a bit earlier. Till then, take care, cheers!

South Africa's Marco Jansen is in for a chat. He says there was nice pace and bounce in the wicket, although not a lot of swing on offer. Shares that once they saw the pace and bounce in the surface, he tried to make full use of it. He reflects that it was a good day for the team and for him personally, and credits the spinners for doing an excellent job when the ball wasn’t doing much for the quicks. He admits he was a bit lucky to be the one who cashed in. Mentions that they thought they would have to field for two days, so today was all about turning up and doing the job. He adds that it is still a good wicket for batting, though the ball is starting to turn a touch, and every now and then one holds in the surface.

Both Kuldeep and Sundar batted together for about half an hour in the final session, but their resistance was cut short sooner by Simon Harmer, and with South Africa opting for the second new ball, the wheels just came off for India. Marco Jansen completed with 6 wickets to his name, while Harmer got a three-fer. The Proteas didn't enforce the follow-on and came out to bat, using a light roller toward the backend of the day. They technically started with 288 runs and Aiden Markram and Ryan Rickelton ensured that they remained unblemished till the end.

The afternoon session started as a nightmare for India. Rishabh Pant departed to a questionable shot when his team desperately needed him to dig in, and Marco Jansen piled on the misery with a sharp short ball barrage. The hosts further collapsed in a heap, all the way down to 122/7. But Washington Sundar and Kuldeep Yadav stemmed the bleeding with some gritty resistance. As the ball got older and softer, it lost that vicious bite from the morning spell. The pitch flattened out sufficiently for batting, and the pair grew more confident, showing that runs were available if you were willing to apply yourself and spend time at the crease.

The opening hour of the morning belonged to India as the openers negotiated the pacers comfortably before Jaiswal started cashing in on the loose deliveries. But the spinners flipped the script completely. Maharaj and Harmer found their rhythm immediately, looping it up perfectly between 75 and 85 clicks, making the ball grip and turn viciously. KL Rahul fell just before drinks, but Jaiswal pushed on to a composed fifty with Sai Sudharsan settling in alongside him. Then disaster struck. Harmer ripped through the middle order with two quick strikes, dismissing both left-handers, and Jurel threw his wicket away with an uninspiring shot, completely misjudging the pace of the surface. Which, in fact, was the case with most of the Indian batters getting out. India tumbled from 95/1 to 102/4 in a flash.

And... that's it for the day. The light has deteriorated and the umps take the players off the field. Another highly absorbing day of cricket comes to a close. It's STUMPS on Day 3 with South Africa well and truly in the driver's seat, dictating all the terms. India have struggled throughout this Test. First, they were made to toil hard with the ball for over 150 overs, and then they couldn't even bat for one full day, and were forced to bowl once again in the twilight. They would have expected to get a couple of wickets, but the Proteas openers just closed that door with sensible batting.
